title: Birthday Problem: k-Way Coincidences
description: Generalizes the Birthday Problem from pairwise collisions to k-way coincidences. Proves the generalized pigeonhole bound, classical recovery (k=2 equals non-injectivity), monotonicity, and probability formulas. Fully proved with 0 axioms and 0 sorries.

meta.assumptions: None. All theorems fully proved from Mathlib.

mathlibDependencies.description: Decomposes set cardinality as sum of fiber cardinalities
Pointwise inequality on summands propagates to sums
A set has more than one element iff it contains two distinct elements

originalContributions: Formalization of k-way coincidences via fiber cardinality
Generalized pigeonhole bound: n > (k-1)*d implies k-way coincidence is certain
Classical recovery: 2-way coincidence is equivalent to non-injectivity
Monotonicity: k-way coincidence implies k'-way for k' <= k
Probability formula and probability = 1 when pigeonhole bound exceeded
Probability monotonicity in k: higher k gives lower probability
Fiber partition of unity: fiber sizes sum to total population

overview.historicalContext: The birthday problem, first posed by Richard von Mises in 1939, asks how many people are needed for a >50% chance of a shared birthday. The natural generalization to k-way coincidences — when do k people share a birthday? — was studied systematically by Flajolet, Gardy, and Thimonier (1992) using analytic combinatorics. The k-way threshold scales as $d^{(k-1)/k} \cdot (k!)^{1/k}$, giving approximately 23, 88, and 187 people for k=2, 3, 4 with d=365. This connects to the classical occupancy problem studied by Feller (1968): distributing n balls into d urns and analyzing the maximum occupancy. In computer science, k-way collisions arise in hash table analysis, distributed load balancing (ensuring no server receives more than k requests), and cryptographic multi-collision attacks studied by Suzuki, Tonien, Kurosawa, and Honda (2006). The generalized pigeonhole principle (Dirichlet's box principle) provides the deterministic threshold: n > (k-1)d guarantees a k-way coincidence regardless of the assignment.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize k-way birthday coincidences: given n people and d days, prove the generalized pigeonhole bound (n > (k-1)*d implies a k-way coincidence is certain), and show the k=2 case recovers the classical birthday problem.
overview.proofStrategy: The proof uses fiber decomposition: each assignment f : Fin n -> Fin d partitions people into fibers by day. The fiber sizes sum to n (partition of unity). The generalized pigeonhole follows by contradiction: if every fiber has < k elements, then n <= (k-1)*d. The classical recovery connects 2-way coincidences to non-injectivity by showing fibers of size >= 2 correspond to collisions.
keyInsights: The fiber decomposition (using Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise) is the key structural tool: it converts the global constraint on n into local constraints on each day
The generalized pigeonhole follows from a simple averaging argument: n people in d bins with each bin having < k means n < k*d
The k=2 classical recovery uses Finset.one_lt_card to extract two distinct elements from a fiber, connecting fiber size >= 2 to non-injectivity
Monotonicity in k is immediate: if some day has >= k people, it certainly has >= k' people for k' <= k
The probability monotonicity follows from set containment: fewer safe assignments for smaller k means higher collision probability

The population bounds (n < k implies probability 0, n > (k-1)d implies probability 1) completely characterize the two extremes, leaving the interesting regime as (k-1) ≤ n ≤ (k-1)d where the probability transitions from 0 to 1
prerequisites: Finite sets and their cardinality (Finset, Fintype)
Basic rational arithmetic and probability as counting

sections.title: Fiber Partition of Unity

sections.title: Generalized Pigeonhole

sections.summary: Shows 2-way coincidence equals non-injectivity, connecting to the standard birthday problem.

sections.title: Monotonicity

sections.title: Trivial Cases
sections.summary: Validates the definition with edge cases: k=0 always satisfied, k=1 iff n > 0.

sections.title: Probability Formula
sections.summary: Defines probKWay, proves it equals 1 when pigeonhole applies, and monotonicity in k.

sections.title: Connection to Classical Birthday Problem
sections.summary: Shows the no-2-way set equals the set of injective functions.

sections.title: Counting Examples
sections.summary: Verifies small cases: 1 person has no 2-way, 0 people have no k-way.

sections.title: Population Bounds
sections.summary: Proves that n < k people cannot have a k-way coincidence, and the probability is 0.

conclusion.summary: Provides a complete formalization of k-way birthday coincidences with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The 25 theorems cover the generalized pigeonhole principle, classical recovery, monotonicity, probability formulas, and counting results.
conclusion.implications: The k-way birthday framework has direct applications in cryptography (multi-collision resistance of hash functions, where Suzuki et al. showed k-collision attacks scale as $O(n^{1-1/k})$ queries), distributed systems (load balancing with maximum-load guarantees), and probabilistic combinatorics (the occupancy problem and its Poisson approximation). The deterministic pigeonhole bound provides hard capacity limits: a hash table with $d$ buckets and $n > (k-1)d$ entries must have a bucket with $k+$ items, regardless of the hash function. The fiber decomposition technique demonstrated here is reusable across occupancy-type problems.
openQuestions: Can the exact threshold for k=3 (approximately n=88 for d=365) be computed using multinomial coefficient sums?
Can the Poisson approximation for k-way coincidences be formalized, connecting to Mathlib's probability theory?
What is the asymptotic scaling of the k-way threshold as a function of k and d?

crossReferences.description: Generalizes from 2-way to k-way coincidences; the classical recovery theorem proves the k=2 case is equivalent to the original birthday problem
The tight collision asymptotics (exp(-k(k-1)/(2n)) bound) complement this combinatorial approach with precise probability estimates
The counting of injective functions (descending factorial) that underlies the birthday probability connects directly to the combinations formula C(d,n)
Both are instances of the pigeonhole principle at different levels: birthday collisions partition people by days, Ramsey theory partitions edges by colors
